title: Black holes big and small appear to follow the same rule when launching jets
freshness: Published September 17, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: When black holes feed on matter, they can blast some of it back into space as powerful jets. A new study finds that black holes ranging from stellar remnants to supermassive giants appear to switch on these jets at the same stages of their feeding cycle, despite their enormous difference in size.
whyItMatters: This suggests that one basic set of physics may govern how all feeding black holes behave, from relatively small ones made by dying stars to the giants at galaxy centres. A rule that works across such different scales turns seemingly erratic black-hole eruptions into something astronomers can begin to predict.

whatToExploreNext: Explore tidal disruption events — rare moments when a star passes too close to a giant black hole and is torn apart, briefly letting astronomers watch the black hole's feeding cycle unfold.

body:
## The slow ones were the problem

A feeding black hole does not keep everything it pulls in. Some of the gas comes back out as a jet, narrow and fast, bright in the radio, and over a long enough time a way to shove gas around in the host galaxy. The suspicion, for years, was that the on-switch looks the same for a stellar-mass black hole and for a supermassive one. The physics of accretion does not know the mass, once you scale the rates properly. Testing that is the annoying part.

Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way swing through a feeding cycle in days or weeks. You can watch a jet turn on. A typical supermassive black hole in an active galaxy changes over thousands of years. No program sits with one system long enough to see it cross the threshold. The comparison has been stuck on that mismatch.

## A torn star as a short film

A Nature Astronomy paper by Adelle Goodwin, of Curtin University’s International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research, and Andrew Mummery, of the Institute for Advanced Study, uses tidal disruption events to get a shorter film. A star passes too close to a supermassive black hole and is shredded. The debris forms a compact disk that can evolve in years rather than millennia. A human career is suddenly long enough.

They assembled optical, ultraviolet, X-ray, and radio data for twenty such events, from telescopes in America, Australia, India, South Africa, and in space. For ten of the twenty, the feeding rate and the timing of the radio outflow could both be modeled well enough to ask a sharp question: at what point in the meal does the jet start?

## Two moments, one of them familiar

There are two launching phases in the sample. The first is early, while the black hole is feeding at super-Eddington rates — more inflow than the limit where outward radiation pressure would balance gravity. The second comes later, hundreds to thousands of days after the disruption, when the feeding rate has fallen to about two percent of that Eddington limit.

The two-percent mark is the result that travels. Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way already change state and launch a compact jet near that same fraction. In the disruption sample, the delayed radio flares cluster around it. The prompt flares cluster at or above the Eddington rate. Goodwin and Mummery argue that one scale-invariant process covers both, across a huge range of black-hole mass. That argument is the interpretation. The clustering of the flares at those two rates is the measurement, and it rests on ten events, not on twenty.

The same split offers a plain account of a known nuisance. Some disruptions launch a jet almost at once. Others go quiet for months or years and then flare in the radio. Those can be one feeding curve, sampled at different times, rather than two species of black hole.

## A forecast, with the holes left visible

If the shared switch is real, a jet launch has a preferred accretion rate, and observers can aim scarce telescopes — the Square Kilometre Array among them — at the moment the rate is due to cross it. The paper’s population check is consistent with that picture, and it should be quoted as a check, not as a new survey. Only a minority of these disks are expected to go super-Eddington, which lines up with prompt-radio detections of roughly 30 to 50 percent. About 40 percent are expected to pass the two-percent threshold inside an observable window of a few years, close to independent estimates of how often the delayed flares appear.

The holes: ten events had data good enough to time both the disk and the outflow. Strongly jetted, relativistic disruptions were left out, because the jet swamps the disk and the feeding rate cannot be measured the same way. The disk model is less trustworthy in the super-Eddington regime. The authors note that this uncertainty would tend to under-predict the feeding rate there, which would not erase the prompt, high-rate group. Launch dates assume a roughly constant outflow speed. Compact jets add more uncertainty.

So the claim to keep is a shared accretion-rate threshold, supported in a carefully modeled handful of disruptions, matching a threshold already used for stellar-mass black holes. It is not a promise that every quiet nucleus will fire on schedule. The Nature Astronomy paper is the fit. The Institute for Advanced Study’s note is Mummery’s institution telling the same story. The next watch is more disruptions, followed as they fade, to see whether the late radio outburst keeps arriving when the rate crosses two percent of Eddington.
